questions.prompt: Ali's teacher corrected his diary. Which sentence from it is correct?
questions.explanation: "get" is irregular and its simple past is "got": I got up at seven. ✓ The trap is to add -ed to every verb: "wake" is irregular (woke, not "waked") and so is "have" (had, not "haved"); "didn't ate" marks the past twice — after didn't the verb goes back to its base form: I didn't eat breakfast.

questions.prompt: Complete the news: "Our school ___ just ___ a new computer room."
questions.explanation: "just" says the action is very recent, with no finished time, so we use the present perfect: has + just + past participle. "Our school" is it, so the auxiliary is "has", and "open" is regular: opened. ✓ The trap is the form after has: it is the past participle (opened), never the base form ("has ... open") or the -ing form ("has ... opening"); and "have" breaks the agreement with "our school".

options.text: She visited Paris two years ago.
She has visited Paris two years ago.
She have visited Paris two years ago.
She visits Paris two years ago.

questions.explanation: "two years ago" gives a finished time, so the simple past is required: She visited Paris two years ago. ✓ The tempting trap is the present perfect: "has visited" can never go with a finished-time expression like "ago" (and "she have" also breaks the agreement). "visits" is present and cannot describe a finished time.

A question with "When…?" asks for a finished time, so it takes the simple past: When + did + subject + base verb. ✓ The trap is the present perfect, "When have you visited…?": the present perfect never goes with a finished time, and "when" asks for one. "did you visited" marks the past twice, and "When you visited…?" has no "did" at all.

"already" between have/has and the past participle signals the present perfect, and the result is visible now (Look!): Salma has already written the report. ✓ The trap is "has ... wrote": after has the verb takes its past participle (written), not its simple past (wrote). "did ... write" is a simple past pattern, and "was ... writing" describes an action in progress, not a finished result.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct pair: "We ___ a lot of tourists in our town lately. Last week, a group from Italy ___ the old market."
questions.explanation: "lately" goes with the present perfect (have seen), while "last week" is a finished time that needs the simple past (visited): We have seen a lot of tourists lately. Last week, a group visited the market. ✓ The trap is to use one tense for both sentences: "has visited" cannot go with "last week", and "saw" does not go with "lately".
